newsitem.title: USA: Austria says Creditanstalt must be sold this year.
newsitem.headline: Austria says Creditanstalt must be sold this year.

text.p: Austria hopes it will finally secure the long-awaited sale of state-owned Creditanstalt-Bankverein by the end of the year, Finance Minister Viktor Klima said on Monday.
"It is clear that this 'never-ending story' must be decided and completed in 1996," Klima said at a briefing held on the sidelines of the annual IMF/World Bank meetings.
The six-year battle over the future ownership of the bank is about to enter a new phase after the only firm bid for the bank failed to result in a deal.

The bid from a consortium led by insurer EA-Generali, and including Germany's Commerzbank and Italy's Banca Commerciale Italiana, foundered as the consortium was reluctant to take on the state's entire 70 percent stake in Creditanstalt.

Commerzbank's chief executive, also in Washington, said on Sunday that the German bank remained interested in Austria's most traditional bank but warned that Austria's price expectations had to be realistic.
"Commerzbank has played a continuous role in the past and will in the future if the terms and conditions fit," Martin Kohlhaussen told a news conference.

The Commerzbank group looks set to compete against Die Erste Oesterreichische SparCasse (First Austrian) in a new round of bidding for Creditanstalt. First Austrian was formerly a partner in the Generali group.
Klima said the call for bids for the company was now being refreshed and would be reissued in the middle of next week. There would then be a four to six-week bidding period.
He added that some of the rules for the offer would be changed so there could be flexibility if bidders did not want to take up all of the 19.9 million shares owned by the state.
"The goal is still to pass the 19.9 million shares to a single bidder," he said. "We want to make this more flexible but the goal remains the same."
Asked about criticism that the ministry was seeking "an Austrian solution", which could cut out foreign bidders, Klima said there were no plans for discrimination.
He added that European Union competition laws had to be taken into account in any decision, "We have to meet not only national conditions but also European ones."

Admitting that the long-drawnout privatization procedure had dragged on for an embarrassingly protracted period ot time, Klima said this was an unfortunate consequence of the strictly laid out laws on privatization.
"That it (the delay in agreeing the sale) is not good for the bank's reputation is clear. That it is not good for Austria's reputation is also clear," Klima said.
"But this is a public sector sale...it cannot take place as it would in the private sector," he said, adding that a private sale allowed much more flexibility over conditions.
Austria is anxious to complete the deal quickly to bring in much-needed revenue.
But Kohlhaussen said Austria may have to be more realistic about the price of the bank if a buyer is to be found.
The government has been targetting a price of 18 billion schillings, based on an assessment by J.P. Morgan. This is well above the current market value of 13 billion schillings.

"We are a private bank," Kohlhaussen said. "Our shareholder policy means acquisitions should be built on solid criteria. There might still be an exaggerated expectation on the price that can be achieved."
